Lesson: Changing the Changes in C, Am, F, G

Four chords, C, Am, F and G, are under more pop songs than any other progression: I, vi, IV, V. It can sound plain, and it can sound rich, depending on what the players do to it. Almost every move is one of four: add a note to each chord, walk the bass between chords, approach a chord with its own dominant, or split a bar into a two-five. This lesson adds those moves one at a time, on the same four bars. The site’s backing band plays every chart on this page, so you can hear each change as it arrives.

How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays four choruses after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument for the whole page, and you can change them while the band plays. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key. (The numerals only name the chord’s root, so a III7 in bar 1 is the dominant of Am, and a vii7 before it is its two.)

1. The basic changes

One bar each of I, vi, IV and V. Plain major and minor triads. The bass moves down a minor third, then down a third, then up a step, and the G at the end pulls back to the C.

Learn this version first. Every other version on the page is this one with something added, so you should be able to hear the plain one underneath.

2. Add extensions

Extensions are notes added on top of the triad without changing what the chord is. Cadd9 adds a D. Am7 adds a G, and Fadd9 adds a G. Gsus2 takes out the B and puts in an A, so the chord has no third: it is neither major nor minor. It sounds suspended, and the ordinary G that follows it, or the C it leads to, feels like the answer.

Use Hear it without the changes to compare with the chart before. The shaded bars are the ones that differ. Listen to bar 4: the leading tone B, which is what pulls G to C, is not there.

3. Add passing chords

Two bars are split in half, so that the bass can walk instead of jump.

  • Bar 1: C, G/B. The bass steps down C, B and arrives on A in bar 2. The G/B is a G chord with its third in the bass.
  • Bar 2: Am, C/G. The bass keeps stepping down, A then G, to land on F in bar 3.
  • Bar 3: F, F♯dim. Now the bass goes up, F, F♯, and arrives on G in bar 4. The F♯dim is built from F♯, A and C, three of the four notes of D7, so it pulls up to G.

Listen to the bass. There is no jump anywhere in the line: every note is one step from the last. A slash chord such as C/G is the C chord with G as its lowest note.

4. Secondary dominants

A dominant seventh chord pulls to the chord a fifth below it. The home key has one, G7, which pulls to C. A secondary dominant is the dominant of some other chord of the key, played just before that chord, so that chord gets to sound like home for a moment.

  • E7 goes to Am. It has a G♯, which is not in the key of C.
  • C7 goes to F. It has a B♭, which is not in the key of C either.
  • D7 goes to G. It has an F♯.
  • G7 goes to C: the usual dominant, now with its seventh.

Each bar now has a note from outside the key, and each of them leads by half step into the next bar’s chord (G♯ to A, B♭ to A, F♯ to G). That is why the progression sounds like it is travelling.

5. ii-V-Is

A dominant can have a chord in front of it, the ii chord, a fifth above, so that the approach itself is a progression: ii, V, then I. Here each secondary dominant gets its own two.

  • Bar 1 keeps C for two beats, then Bm7 E7, a two-five into Am.
  • Bar 2 keeps Am for two beats, then Gm7 C7, a two-five into F.
  • Bar 3 is Fmaj7 for two beats, then Am7 D7, a two-five into G.
  • Bar 4 stays on G7.

Strictly, the two-five into a minor chord uses a half-diminished ii (Bm7♭5), but plain Bm7 is the common way to write it in pop and the band plays it as written. Compare the last chord of each of the first three bars with section 4: it is the same dominant, with a two in front.

Build your own chorus

Choose one option for each bar and the chart rewrites itself. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. All of the options fit together, so there is no wrong combination: try a plain first bar with a busy last bar, or the reverse.

Test your ear

The band plays the plain four bars with one bar changed. The question tells you which bar to listen to. Pick what you heard.

Where to go next

  • Play along. Set the strip at the bottom to Loop, pick a key and play or sing over each version in turn. The bars with new chords are the ones that ask for new notes.
  • Take a chorus you built to Tools → Backing Track (use Copy as ABC above and paste it into Edit the changes (ABC) there) to choose the bass line, comping rhythm and drum groove.
  • Learn each version in the keys you play most: C, G, D and A for guitar and voice.
